lesson.title: Distributing Across Every Term: Multiplying Polynomials
lesson.summary: Multiplying two polynomials means distributing every term of one across every term of the other, then combining like terms to reach the simplified product.
lesson.body:
When you multiply two polynomials, you are really just applying the distributive property more than once. Recall that the distributive property says a(b + c) = ab + ac: a single term gets multiplied across a sum. A polynomial is nothing more than a sum of terms, so when you multiply a polynomial by another polynomial, every term in the first one has to distribute across every term in the second one. There is no shortcut that skips this step; multiplying polynomials is simply the distributive property applied systematically until every pair of terms has been multiplied.

The reliable process has two stages. First, multiply each term of the first polynomial by each term of the second polynomial, keeping track of the exponent rule x^a times x^b equals x^(a+b). Second, once all of those products are written out, combine any like terms, terms with the same variable raised to the same power, to write the answer in simplest form. Skipping the second stage is one of the most common student errors: the unsimplified sum of products is correct but incomplete. It does not matter which polynomial you treat as the one being distributed, since multiplication is commutative; either order reaches the same product. Many students find it helpful to organize the work in a box or table, one row for each term of the first polynomial and one column for each term of the second, filling in every cell with that row's term times that column's term before combining anything.

Consider multiplying (x + 3) by (x^2 - 2x + 5). Distribute x across the trinomial: x times x^2 is x^3, x times negative 2x is negative 2x^2, and x times 5 is 5x. Then distribute 3 across the same trinomial: 3 times x^2 is 3x^2, 3 times negative 2x is negative 6x, and 3 times 5 is 15. Writing every product together gives x^3 - 2x^2 + 5x + 3x^2 - 6x + 15. Combining like terms, negative 2x^2 and 3x^2 combine to x^2, and 5x and negative 6x combine to negative x, leaving a final answer of x^3 + x^2 - x + 15. Check this by substituting x = 2: the original expression gives (2 + 3)(4 - 4 + 5) = 5 times 5 = 25, and the simplified answer gives 8 + 4 - 2 + 15 = 25, confirming the work is correct.

Notice something useful about degree here: the first polynomial had degree 1 and the second had degree 2, and the product has degree 3, which is 1 + 2. This will always happen when you multiply two nonzero polynomials, because the highest degree term in the product comes only from multiplying the highest degree terms of each factor together, and that product cannot cancel with anything else. You can also predict how many raw products you will get before combining: a polynomial with m terms times a polynomial with n terms produces m times n products. In the example above, a 2 term polynomial times a 3 term polynomial produced 2 times 3, or 6, raw products, even though two pairs of them combined into fewer terms in the final answer.

Binomial times binomial, a two term polynomial times another two term polynomial, comes up so often that it earns its own memorable shortcut. That special case, covered next, is called the FOIL method, and it is nothing more than this same distributive process with exactly four products to keep track of instead of many.
